# Stegobench

> Measure how good a steganography detector is, using images whose answers
> are already known. Build a labelled corpus, run detectors over identical
> bytes, and report numbers somebody else can check.
>
> It does NOT examine unlabelled images to find out what is in them. That is
> the opposite direction, and there is no command for it. See "The question
> this tool does not answer" below before routing a user here.

This file is for a model deciding whether and how to call this tool. It
describes what exists today, not a roadmap. Every command listed below is
built and tested; nothing is named here that you cannot call.

## What this is, in one paragraph

`stegobench` runs steganography detectors and embedders as sandboxed plugins
(Docker containers pinned by digest, or a locally installed binary pinned by
its SHA-256), scores them against a labelled corpus, and emits a versioned
JSON document (`result-v1`) that names the exact bytes it was measured on, the
exact plugin version it ran, and whether anything failed. It does not embed
or detect anything itself: it is a harness, and the tools it runs, including
Stegcore, are registered exactly the same way a stranger's tool would be.

## Command vocabulary (what actually exists)

Every subcommand takes `--json`, which puts machine-readable output on stdout
and leaves human text on stderr, so `stegobench ... --json | jq` works while
progress still reaches a terminal.

- `stegobench schema <result-v1|run-v1|manifest-v1|all>`: print a JSON Schema
  generated from the Rust types that actually write these documents.
- `stegobench validate <file>`: check a document against whichever of the
  three schemas its own `schema` field names; exits 6 on a mismatch.
- `stegobench verify <file> --corpus DIR`: recompute the corpus digest a
  result claims and say whether the document and the corpus are about each
  other; exits 5 when they are not.
- `stegobench report <paths...>`: render one or many result documents as a
  text, Markdown or CSV table for an evaluation write-up, with the pairing
  verdict, the split verdict, the corpus digest and the named-or-custom
  configuration on each row rather than in a legend. It refuses to put
  results from different corpora in one table, sections `custom` runs off
  under a sentence saying what they can be compared with, and never orders
  by score.
- `stegobench list <detectors|embedders|corpora|all>`: everything a registry
  can run, plus the datasets it knows about, read live from the registry, so
  it cannot go stale. The output names which registry answered.
- `stegobench describe <name>`: one tool's full registered manifest, or one
  corpus's, whichever the name belongs to. A corpus entry records where the
  dataset lives, what its terms say, who established that and on what date,
  and whether images derived from it may be republished. Terms nobody has
  read are marked unverified rather than guessed at, and republication is
  refused on anything unverified.
- `stegobench fetch <corpus> --tier <TIER>`: download one tier of a registered
  corpus over the route its registry entry declares, and check the bytes
  against the SHA-256 and the size that entry declared in advance. A corpus
  whose terms do not permit redistribution is refused before anything opens,
  because fetching it on a user's behalf would make this project the mirror;
  exits 7 for that, 3 where there is no route to fetch, 5 where what arrived is
  not what was declared. It resumes an interrupted download and never leaves a
  half-written file at the path that means verified. It does not unpack: it
  reports one verified file and what it is. `curl` carries the bytes.
- `stegobench doctor`: checks whether this machine can run what the registry
  claims. With self-tests enabled (the default) it asks each present tool to
  score a known planted signal and a known clean fixture, because a tool that
  is merely installed is not a tool that works.
- `stegobench completions <bash|zsh|fish|powershell>`: shell completion script.
- `stegobench help <scope|pairing|splits|licences|plugins|results|reports>`:
  the reasoning behind the harness's hard rules, written for a reader who
  never opens the repo. `scope` is the one to read first: it separates
  measuring a detector from examining your own images.
- `stegobench score --corpus <DIR> --detector <NAME>`: asks the detector
  about every sample under the directory and writes a `result-v1` document.
  `--detector` is repeatable and `all` means every registered detector; with
  more than one, `--out` and `--records` name directories and each detector
  gets its own file and its own records file inside them. Exit 0 means every
  detector asked for produced a result, 3 that at least one was unavailable,
  4 that at least one failed, so 0 never means "some".
  Resumable, per detector: every answer lands in a records file as it is
  produced, and the same command run again continues rather than restarting.
  It reads an unpacked corpus directory, and marks every such run `custom`,
  because a directory carries no digest anybody can check. A tiny corpus
  ships in the clone at `corpora/starter` (six covers, twelve stego images)
  so a fresh install has something to score; it is a demonstration and a
  number from it must not be quoted.
- `stegobench plan <command>`: what that command would cost, without running
  it. Takes the command as you would type it, so
  `stegobench plan score --corpus D --detector N`. Reports the item count, the
  estimated time where the tool declares a rate, and the worst case if every
  item hits the deadline. Where no rate is declared it says so rather than
  inventing a figure.

## The question this tool does not answer

A user who asks "are these images hiding something" wants a detector pointed
at their own files, not a benchmark. Stegobench has no command for that and
should not be made to look as though it does.

`stegobench check` and `stegobench scan` exist only as signposts: they refuse,
with exit code 2, and explain the difference. Pointing `score` at a directory
of images with no records beside them refuses too, with exit code 3, for the
same reason. Neither is a feature to work around.

What to do instead: `stegobench list detectors` names every registered
detector and `stegobench describe <name>` says where each one lives and how it
is run. Run one of those directly on the user's files, and read its own
documentation for what its output means.

## Where the registry comes from

In order: `--registry` or `STEGOBENCH_REGISTRY`, then `./plugins/registry`,
then beside the executable, then the per-user data directory, then the system
data directory, and finally a copy compiled into the binary. An installed
binary therefore works from any directory with no configuration. A path named
explicitly is used as given: if it is not there that is exit code 1, never a
silent fall back to a different registry. `stegobench doctor --json` reports
the resolved path and how it was found under `registry`.

Registries are not merged. The first one found answers in full, so a directory
holding a single entry yields a single tool. Do not tell a user to create a
registry directory containing only their own tool unless that is what they
want; tell them to copy `plugins/registry/` and add to the copy.

## Exit codes (a contract, not incidental)

`0` success · `1` generic failure · `2` usage error · `3` pre-flight refusal ·
`4` plugin failure · `5` verification mismatch · `6` schema invalid ·
`7` licence refusal · `8` environment unfit · `130` interrupted.

Codes 3 and 7 mean the tool is capable of the thing and is declining. Do not
retry a 3 or a 7 unchanged; read the message, which names the reason.

## Where the schemas live

`stegobench schema <name>` is the source of truth; the types themselves are
in `crates/stegobench-core/src/{result,run,manifest}.rs`. A document you did
not generate yourself should be checked with `stegobench validate` before you
trust anything in it, because a result naming a corpus that has since changed
is exactly the failure `validate` exists to catch.

## The rules that are not obvious from the flags

Read via `stegobench help <topic>` rather than restated in full here, because
the tool itself is the source of truth for its own reasoning:

- `pairing`: why a clean cover and its stego twin must differ in nothing but
  the payload, and what happens to a result when they do not.
- `splits`: why a cover and every stego image made from it must land on the
  same side of a train/test split.
- `licences`: why every corpus row carries its own licence rather than one
  for the whole collection.
- `plugins`: why a detector or embedder is a TOML registry entry pinned by
  digest or by executable hash, never code wired into the harness.
- `scope`: what this measures and what it does not, and where to send a user
  who wants the other thing.

## What an agent should not do here

- Do not call `plan` expecting the run to happen. It estimates and returns;
  nothing is scored and nothing is written. See "Command vocabulary" above.
- Do not treat a registry entry's `image.reference` as safe to run without a
  digest. `stegobench` itself refuses to load one that is not: see `plugins`
  in `stegobench help plugins`.
- Do not publish anything on a corpus's behalf. There is no publish command
  exposed to an agent surface in this version, and none should be inferred.
- Do not invent a schema version or a field. `stegobench validate` is the
  only source of truth for whether a document is well formed.
